procedural_history.impugned_order: The High Court reversed the Trial Court's verdict of conviction of the respondent-accused under Section 376 I.P.C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Trial Court convicted the respondent-accused under Section 376 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo sentence of ten years of rigorous imprisonment and also imposed a fine of Rs.25,000/-. In appeal, the High Court reversed the verdict of conviction of the respondent-accused only on the ground that the opinion of Dr. Neerja Gupta (PW-6) and Dr. Pooja Gupta (PW-7) are not conclusive to hold that the respondent-accused has forcefully committed sexual intercourse with the prosecutrix. The High Court held that the evidence of the prosecutrix (PW-4) does not inspire the confidence of the court to sustain the conviction and the respondent-accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt and on those findings the High Court has reversed the judgment of the Trial Court and set aside the conviction and sentence of the imprisonment imposed upon respondent-accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Himachal Pradesh appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court Legal Services Committee nominated an amicus curiae to represent the respondent-accused, who did not appear despite service of notice. The Supreme Court heard arguments from both sides and reviewed the High Court's judgment, witness evidence, and other materials.

decision.sentence_status: Sentence of ten years imprisonment restored
directions: The impugned judgment and order of the High Court is set aside.
The respondent-accused is to surrender to custody within a period of four weeks from today to serve the remaining sentence failing which he shall be taken to custody.
A copy of this order be sent to the concerned trial court for necessary action.

issue.issue_text: Whether the absence of injuries on the private parts of a child prosecutrix and an intact hymen is sufficient to disprove the charge of rape.

facts: The prosecutrix was a nine-year-old child.
A medical examination conducted by Dr. Neerja Gupta (PW-6) found no injuries on the prosecutrix's private parts.
The doctor opined that in cases of "slightest or small penetration, hymen will not rupture" and that a hymen would only rupture in cases of "complete penetration with force."
The High Court had acquitted the accused, partly on the grounds that this medical evidence was not conclusive proof of sexual intercourse.
law: The act of inserting a private part into the private part of another person constitutes rape, and even slight penetration is sufficient.
It is a well-settled legal principle that it is not necessary for external injuries to be found on the body of a prosecutrix to prove a charge of rape.
The sole testimony of a prosecutrix can be sufficient to sustain a conviction if it inspires the confidence of the court.
application: The Supreme Court relied on the expert medical testimony of Dr. Neerja Gupta (PW-6), who stated that the absence of a ruptured hymen or injuries does not rule out sexual intercourse, as slight penetration may not cause such injuries.
The Court reasoned that the accused's act of inserting his private part into the prosecutrix's private part constituted rape, and this act may not have been forceful enough to rupture the hymen.
It concluded that in the facts and circumstances of the case, particularly given the victim's young age and credible testimony, the absence of injuries on her private parts was "of no consequence."
The Court held that the lack of physical injury cannot be a reason to disbelieve the prosecutrix's testimony or to conclude that the incident did not take place.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition, holding that the absence of injuries on the private parts of a child prosecutrix and an intact hymen is not sufficient to disprove the charge of rape. The Court reasoned that even slight penetration constitutes rape and may not cause physical injuries, and therefore, the lack of such medical evidence cannot invalidate the credible testimony of the victim.

issue.issue_text: Whether the testimony of a child prosecutrix in a rape case can be disbelieved solely on the basis of medical evidence that does not show signs of complete penetration or injury.

facts: A nine-year-old girl (the prosecutrix) accused her cousin of repeatedly committing sexual intercourse with her while she was staying at her aunt's house.
A medical examination of the prosecutrix found no injuries on her private parts and her hymen was not ruptured.
The Trial Court convicted the accused, finding the girl's testimony convincing.
The High Court overturned the conviction, giving the accused the benefit of the doubt, partly because the medical evidence was not conclusive and did not show signs of forceful intercourse.
law: The conviction in a rape case can be sustained on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix if it inspires confidence.
Corroboration of a prosecutrix's testimony is not a requirement of law but a guidance of prudence.
The absence of external injuries on the prosecutrix is not conclusive proof that rape did not occur, as penetration alone is sufficient to constitute the offense.
The testimony of a child victim should be evaluated carefully, but there is no reason to view it with doubt or suspicion, especially when there is no motive for false implication.
application: The Court found the testimony of the nine-year-old prosecutrix to be credible and reliable, noting she had no reason to falsely implicate her cousin. Her reluctance to return to her aunt's house and her complaint to her teachers supported her credibility.
The Court relied on the expert medical testimony of Dr. Neerja Gupta (PW-6), who stated that "slightest or small penetration" might not rupture the hymen or cause injury.
The Court reasoned that the act described by the prosecutrix—the accused inserting his private part into hers—constitutes rape, regardless of whether it resulted in physical injury.
Therefore, the Court held that the lack of injury or a ruptured hymen was "of no consequence" and could not be used as a reason to disbelieve the child's otherwise convincing testimony.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that a child prosecutrix's testimony could be disbelieved solely because of inconclusive medical evidence. It held that the absence of injuries or a ruptured hymen does not disprove rape, especially when the victim is a child and the penetration may have been slight. Since the child's testimony was found to be credible and confidence-inspiring, it was sufficient on its own to uphold the conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the non-examination of a witness who is a close relative of both the prosecutrix and the accused is fatal to the prosecution's case.

facts: The witness in question was the aunt of the prosecutrix.
This same witness was also the mother of the accused.
The prosecution did not examine the aunt as a witness.
The defense argued that this non-examination was fatal to the prosecution's case.
law: When a potential witness is a close relative of the accused, the prosecution's failure to examine them is not necessarily a fatal flaw.
In such circumstances, the accused has the option to examine the relative as a defense witness if they believe the testimony would be favorable to their case.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the unexamined witness was the mother of the accused.
The Court reasoned that nothing prevented the accused from calling his own mother to testify as a witness for the defense.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the failure of the prosecution to examine the aunt could not be held against them or considered fatal to their case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the non-examination of the aunt was not fatal to the prosecution's case. The Court reasoned that since the witness was the accused's mother, the accused could have called her to testify if her evidence was beneficial to him. The onus was not solely on the prosecution to examine a witness so closely related to the accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether an acquittal can be based on any doubt, or if it must be a 'reasonable doubt' in cases of sexual assault.

facts: The High Court had reversed a trial court's conviction in a sexual assault case, acquitting the accused by giving him the "benefit of doubt".
law: The Supreme Court stated the legal principle that in order to give the benefit of doubt to an accused, the doubt "has to be a reasonable doubt."

The Court cited its previous ruling in *State of Rajasthan v. N.K. The Accused*, which held that a doubt in criminal law "has to be a reasonable doubt and not an excuse for a finding in favour of acquittal."
application: The Court applied this principle to the current case, finding that the High Court was not justified in reversing the conviction.
It noted that courts have a great responsibility to be sensitive when dealing with sexual assault charges and that "unmerited acquittals" are a serious problem.
After reviewing the evidence, particularly the victim's credible testimony, the Supreme Court determined that the High Court's reasons for doubt were not reasonable or convincing.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an acquittal cannot be based on any doubt; it must be a 'reasonable doubt'. Because the High Court's acquittal was not based on a reasonable doubt, the Supreme Court set aside the acquittal and restored the conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the absence of injuries on the private parts of a child prosecutrix and an intact hymen is sufficient to disprove the charge of rape.
appellant_arguments: The absence of injuries or a ruptured hymen does not disprove sexual intercourse, as stated by the medical expert (PW-6).
The doctor (PW-6) specifically opined that in cases of 'slightest or small penetration, hymen will not rupture'.
The High Court erred by using the lack of physical injury as a reason to disbelieve the prosecutrix and acquit the accused.
respondent_arguments: The medical evidence from Dr. Neerja Gupta (PW-6) and Dr. Pooja Gupta (PW-7) was not conclusive in proving that the prosecutrix was subjected to forceful sexual intercourse.
The lack of injury on the private parts creates doubt about the prosecution's claim of rape.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the testimony of a child prosecutrix in a rape case can be disbelieved solely on the basis of medical evidence that does not show signs of complete penetration or injury.
appellant_arguments: The conviction can be sustained on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix if it inspires confidence, and corroboration is not a requirement of law.

The Trial Court, which had the opportunity to observe the prosecutrix (PW-4), found her evidence convincing and confidence-inspiring, and the High Court should not have interfered with this finding without a convincing reason.
The prosecutrix was a young girl of nine with no reason to falsely implicate the respondent, who was her cousin.
Her testimony was corroborated by her conduct, such as her reluctance to return to her aunt's house and her complaint to her teachers (PW-1 and PW-2).
respondent_arguments: The testimony of the prosecutrix (PW-4) does not inspire the confidence of the court and is therefore insufficient to sustain a conviction.
The lack of conclusive medical evidence to support the prosecutrix's claims makes her testimony unreliable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an acquittal can be based on any doubt, or if it must be a 'reasonable doubt' in cases of sexual assault.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred in giving the respondent the benefit of doubt, as its doubt was based on a misappreciation of the evidence.
The High Court incorrectly found the prosecutrix's testimony unconvincing and gave undue weight to the inconclusive medical evidence, creating a doubt that was not reasonable.
The evidence, when properly appreciated, established the accused's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
respondent_arguments: The accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt because the prosecution's case was not proven conclusively.
The doubt arose from the combination of the prosecutrix's testimony not inspiring confidence and the medical evidence failing to corroborate the allegation of rape.

cases.case_name: State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh and Others
cases.principle: The conviction in a rape case can be sustained on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix if it inspires confidence, and corroboration is not a requirement of law but a guidance of prudence.

cases.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. N.K. The Accused
cases.principle: In order to give the benefit of doubt to the accused, it has to be a reasonable doubt.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for rape can be sustained on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix if it inspires the confidence of the court, as corroboration is not a requirement of law. The absence of physical injuries on the victim is not conclusive proof that sexual intercourse did not occur and cannot be the sole reason to disbelieve the prosecutrix's testimony. An appellate court ought not to interfere with a trial court's finding of fact regarding the credibility of a witness unless there are convincing reasons to do so.
obiter: In order to give the benefit of doubt to the accused, it has to be a reasonable doubt.
Since at the time of incident the victim was at her tender age, there is no reason to show sympathy towards the respondent-accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court erred in reversing the respondent-accused's conviction by misapplying the standard for reasonable doubt and improperly discrediting the child prosecutrix's testimony based on inconclusive medical evidence. The court found that the sole testimony of the nine-year-old victim was confidence-inspiring and sufficient for conviction, as the Trial Court had correctly determined. The absence of physical injuries or a ruptured hymen is not dispositive proof that rape did not occur, especially in cases of slight penetration, and cannot be the basis for overturning a conviction grounded in credible testimony.
legal_tests_applied: The conviction can be sustained on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix, if it inspires confidence. Corroboration of the testimony of the prosecutrix is not a requirement of law; but a guidance of prudence under the given facts and circumstances.
In order to give the benefit of doubt to the accused, it has to be a reasonable doubt.

When the Trial Court which had the opportunity of seeing and hearing the witness has held that the evidence of the prosecutrix inspires confidence of the court, in the absence of any convincing reason, the High Court ought not to have interfered with such finding of fact.
why_respondent_won: The High Court's finding that the prosecutrix's evidence did not inspire confidence was incorrect; the Supreme Court held that the Trial Court, which had the opportunity to observe the witness, correctly found her testimony convincing, and as a nine-year-old girl, she had no reason to falsely implicate her cousin.

The High Court's reliance on medical evidence to create doubt was an error, as the absence of injuries is not conclusive. The court accepted the medical expert's (PW-6) opinion that 'in case of small/slightest penetration the hymen will not rupture' and stated, 'The absence of injuries on the private part of the prosecutrix can be of no consequence in the facts and circumstances of the present case.'

The High Court misapplied the benefit of doubt standard. The Supreme Court clarified that a doubt 'has to be a reasonable doubt and not an excuse for a finding in favour of acquittal,' which the High Court's doubt was not.
The non-examination of the aunt, who was the mother of the accused, was not fatal to the prosecution's case, as the accused could have examined her as his own witness.
policy_considerations: Courts must remain alive to the fact that in a case of rape, no self-respecting woman would come forward in a court just to make a humiliating statement against her honour.
Seeking corroboration of a victim's statement as a rule in such cases amounts to adding insult to injury.
Courts have to display a greater sense of responsibility and to be more sensitive while dealing with the charges of sexual assault on woman.
An unmerited acquittal encourages wolves in the society being on the prowl for easy prey, more so when the victims are gullible, young and innocent.
